approved: Superannuation Legislation Amendment (Reform of Self Managed Superannuation Funds Supervisory Levy Arrangements) Bill 2013

Introduced a bill raising the self managed superannuation fund supervisory levy cap from $200 to $300, with the actual levy rising to $259 from the 2013 to 2014 income year, and said the number of such funds grew by more than 27 per cent to over 478,000 between June 2008 and June 2012.

Tabled the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services' advisory report, including a dissenting report, on the Superannuation Legislation Amendment (Reform of Self Managed Superannuation Funds Supervisory Levy Arrangements) Bill.

Presented the committee's report recommending passage of the bill raising the cap on the self-managed super fund supervisory levy, noting the levy will actually rise to $259 as the number of self-managed funds, now over 478,000, keeps growing.

Argued the government's justification for raising the self-managed super fund levy cap is misleading, noting Australian Taxation Office officers confirmed the levy already collects enough to cover the agency's approximately $85 million annual cost of regulating the sector, contradicting the bill's explanatory memorandum.

Opposed elements of the Superannuation Legislation Amendment bill that raises the self-managed super fund levy from $191 to $259 while also bringing forward payment, meaning funds will pay $321 in 2013-14 and $388 in 2014-15, called it a revenue grab following more than $8 billion ripped from superannuation since Labor took office in November 2007, and noted the government has delivered five budget deficits from five budgets despite promising a surplus.

Argued for the Superannuation Legislation Amendment bill, noting the average self-managed super fund held $963,002 in assets as at June 2011 against a new $259 annual levy, and defended the government's lift in the compulsory superannuation guarantee from nine to 12 per cent, projected to give a 30-year-old on average earnings about $110,000 more by retirement and benefit 8.4 million Australians.

Opposed the Superannuation Legislation Amendment bill, calling the levy's increase to $259, a 35.6 per cent rise and the largest since it moved from $45 to $150 in 2006-07, an unjustified cash grab, noting a Tax Office official told the committee inquiry the current levy 'broadly' covers its roughly $85 million annual supervision cost despite the government's claim it does not, and detailed projected revenue of $70 million, $164 million and $88 million over the following three years.

Opposed the Superannuation Legislation Amendment bill as part of a pattern of instability, citing more than $8 billion ripped from superannuation over five years and 23 separate changes to the system, and read constituent letters warning that while $500,000 once sufficed for a couple's retirement, advisers now recommend at least $1 million to generate an annual income of $55,000 to $65,000.

Summing up debate on the Superannuation Legislation Amendment bill, explained it will help fund the ATO's SMSF Stronger Super reforms, announced a cost recovery impact statement documenting the levy's compliance with government guidelines will be published on the ATO website by 1 July 2013, and tabled a correction updating the bill's financial impact estimates.

The Superannuation Legislation Amendment (Reform of Self Managed Superannuation Funds Supervisory Levy Arrangements) Bill 2013 increases the maximum SMSF supervisory levy from $200 to $300 per year, with an actual levy of $259 from 2013-14, and changes collection timing so the levy is paid in the same financial year, phased in over two years, to fully recover the ATO's regulatory costs for the growing SMSF sector (478,000 funds as of June 2012, up 27% since 2008).

The Coalition criticised the Superannuation Legislation Amendment (Reform of Self Managed Superannuation Funds Supervisory Levy Arrangements) Bill 2013 as an Orwellian Labor cash grab and blamed Treasurer Wayne Swan's fiscal mismanagement, but nonetheless chose not to oppose the bill.
